title: Legal Pay Per Call: How Law Firms Buy Calls
h1: Legal pay per call: how law firms buy calls
description: Legal pay per call explained: how law firms buy inbound calls, which rules make a call payable, and how to route calls to the right firm.
faq: How does pay per call work for lawyers?

A law firm agrees a price for each qualified inbound call from someone who needs legal help. Calls are routed live to the firm's intake team, and only calls that meet the agreed rules, such as state, practice area and minimum length, are billed.
What makes a legal call billable?

It is set in the agreement between buyer and seller. Common rules are a minimum call duration in seconds, a caller in a state the firm covers, a matter in the firm's practice area, and no repeat calls from the same person within a set period.
Can law firms buy calls only from certain states?
Yes. Campaigns can use state targeting and buyer state rules so that only callers from the states a firm covers are routed to it, and other calls go to a different buyer.
body:
Legal pay per call is a way for law firms to pay for inbound phone calls from people who need a lawyer, instead of paying for clicks or form fills. The firm agrees a price per qualified call, sets the rules for which calls count (practice area, state, minimum call length, office hours), and the call is routed live to its intake team. Firms like it because a phone call from someone who was just in an accident or just received a court notice is usually closer to signing than a web form. The catch is that the rules have to be written down and enforced by software, or every invoice becomes an argument.

How law firms buy calls

A law firm usually buys calls in one of two ways: directly from a publisher who runs ads, or through a network that collects calls from many affiliates and sells them to several firms. Either way, the same pieces need to be agreed before the first call is sent:

  • Practice area. Personal injury, workers' compensation, family law, criminal defence and other areas are usually separate offers with separate prices.
  • States. A firm can only take cases where its lawyers can practise, so calls from other states should never reach it.
  • Payable call length. A minimum duration, agreed in seconds, decides when a call becomes billable.
  • Hours and capacity. Intake teams have opening hours and a limit on how many calls they can handle per day.
  • Repeat callers. The same person calling twice in a week should not be billed twice.

What makes a legal call worth paying for

Legal calls tend to carry higher payouts than many other verticals, which is exactly why quality control matters. A good legal call is a real person, in a state the firm covers, describing a matter the firm handles, who stays on the line long enough for intake to qualify them. A bad one is a wrong number, a caller looking for a different kind of help, or a source that sends a burst of short calls.

Three things help firms and sellers agree on quality:

  1. Recordings or transcripts. When a call is disputed, both sides can check what was actually said rather than arguing from memory.
  2. A pre-transfer check. Before a call is passed to the firm, the system confirms the firm is open, under its cap and able to take that call. If not, the call goes to the next buyer instead of ringing an empty office.
  3. Source grading. Each traffic source is watched over time, and sources that send too many short calls are paused before they waste the firm's budget.

Routing legal calls to the right firm

Most legal campaigns have more than one buyer. A network might work with several firms in different states, or several firms in the same state with different caps. Two routing methods are common:

  • Waterfall routing. Buyers are tried in a set order. If the first firm is closed, capped or blocked for that caller's state, the call moves to the next one. This suits fixed-price agreements. Our campaign setup guide walks through building one.
  • Real-time bidding. Buyers are asked for a price at the moment the call comes in, and the highest bid above a minimum wins. This suits firms that want to pay more for calls they value most. See how real-time call bidding works for the details.

Compliance questions to settle first

Legal advertising and call recording both come with rules, and they vary by state and by how the calls are generated. Common questions include whether callers need to hear a recording notice, how do-not-call requests are handled, and what the ads that generate the calls are allowed to say. This article is not legal advice. Both firms and call sellers should check their obligations with their own counsel before sending live traffic, and write the agreed answers into the campaign rules.

How to run legal pay per call in Insight Dial

Here is how the setup above maps to Insight Dial:

  1. Create the campaign for one practice area and set state targeting so only callers in the firm's states are routed to it.
  2. Add each firm as a buyer with its hours, daily cap, state rules and minimum payable duration. Turn on repeat-caller blocks and add any blocked numbers.
  3. Choose routing: a waterfall with a pre-transfer check, or real-time bidding, where buyers are pinged in parallel and a fall-back applies if nobody bids.
  4. Give each affiliate a tracking number (with dynamic number insertion on landing pages) and a payout rate, so every call is credited to its source.
  5. Switch on recordings with a spoken recording notice where your rules need one, and AI transcription with one-line summaries if it is enabled on your account.
  6. Watch quality grades (Good, Watch, Poor). Sources sending too many short calls can be paused automatically.
  7. Give firms a buyer portal where they can see their calls and download statements, and use the test-call tool before going live.

Pricing is pay as you go: a per-minute call rate plus a monthly price per tracking number, taken from a topped-up balance. Details are on the pricing page, and other verticals are covered in the industries hub, including our page on legal pay per call.

Start with one practice area

The simplest way to begin is one practice area, one or two firms and a short list of trusted sources. Get the payable-call rules agreed, run test calls, then add volume. Once the numbers match on both sides, adding more firms or states is a routing change, not a rebuild.
